To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the vastness (and hence the explorable size) of protein sequence space can be quantified and that the vastness is so great that all of it has been explored by the Earth’s organisms during its 4 Gyrs of existence.
the vastness and explorable-ness of protein sequence spaces are two different things.

the vastness and complexity of sequence space is actually not a barrier to its full exploration, but that instead, the vastness of sequence space is a barrier to its exploration only when we consider the number of organisms that have ever existed on Earth, which is very small, and the number of distinct classes of amino acid, which is very large.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: how much of sequence space has been occupied by life?
the question of whether the vastness of the protein sequence space is a barrier to life's exploration of the space, and we conclude that this is not the case.
the extent of protein sequence space that has been explored and occupied by life on the Earth.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there are no limits on the extent to which sequence space can be explored, but that the number of distinct classes of amino acid that can be explored is very small, perhaps only 10–12, and that this is the real limitation.
life has not explored only a tiny part of protein sequence space, but has instead explored all of protein sequence space.
the vast majority of protein sequence space, and hence of the possible functional classes of protein molecules, have been explored by natural selection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no such thing as the space of possible proteins; there are just proteins.
the vastness and complexity of sequence space has no role to play in explaining the origin of life or the evolution of biological complexity.
life is not contingent on the details of protein sequence space, rather, it is a consequence of the vastness of this space.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the vast majority of the protein sequence space that is accessible to life on Earth can be explored by the evolutionary process.
the evolution of life on Earth is not constrained by the vastness of sequence space but instead is constrained by the limited number of functionally unique classes of amino acids.
the number of function classes of amino acids is the key parameter in determining the number of distinct protein sequences that have been explored by life.
